speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment with countries curbing the export of their produce (a) what measures are in place to ensure Singapore’s continued supply of key food items; (b) what further measures will be taken to prevent future disruptions to Singapore’s food supply; and (c) what support can be extended to businesses and consumers to help manage the impact and rising costs as a result of disruptions to food supply.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam
text: asked the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (a) whether the Ministry has been informed in advance of the Malaysian authorities’ decision to stop cross-border supply of fresh chickens; and (b) how has this month-long suspension affected local businesses thus far.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: My response will also address Parliamentary Questions filed by Mr Edward Chia1 and Mr Shawn Huang2 due for reading at subsequent Sittings, and I would like to invite the Members to ask any supplementary questions they may have.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Disruptions to the production, export or transportation of agricultural inputs or food products in one country or region often have knock-on effects on other parts of the food supply chain.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These can arise from many causes, including geopolitical tensions, extreme weather events, disruptions to logistics chains or policy decisions by foreign governments.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Some food producing countries have reacted by imposing exports bans or restrictions on food items.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Indonesia's recent palm oil export ban, India's wheat and sugar export bans and Malaysia's chicken export ban, are recent examples.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, we have adopted a multi-pronged approach to mitigate the impacts.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: First, we work with the industry to build resilience in their supply networks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA supports the industry's diversification efforts by actively accrediting multiple overseas food sources.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA also helps to accredit new source countries, regions and suppliers in order to give our importers more choices.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Through import licensing, SFA requires egg importers to have a business continuity plan and have measures such as diversifying import sources, signing retainer contracts or holding a buffer stock.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These measures help to mitigate the impact of disruptions from any single source.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We currently import our food from over 170 countries and regions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: This has dropped by three percentage points from 37% in 2018.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Frozen chicken provides us with greater food resilience as industrial freezing extends the shelf life of the meat.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Under proper storage conditions, frozen meat can be kept for up to a year.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It enlarges our pool of available choices to include suppliers from countries that are further away like Brazil and the United States.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In the recent chicken export ban, we saw industry partners such as SATS and trade associations such as the Meat Traders Association and the Poultry Merchants Association, increase imports of frozen chicken from the United States and Brazil, and chilled chicken from Thailand and Australia.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA has also recently accredited Indonesia as a new source for the import of chicken.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked if there were constraints to expanding the number of approved countries for poultry imports.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Even as we diversify our food sources, food safety remains paramount.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Only accredited sources that meet Singapore's food safety and animal health standards will be allowed to export to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Louis Chua asked whether we have plans to accelerate "30 by 30".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The 30 by 30 goal is already very ambitious.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We only have about 1% of our land set aside for agri-food production, given other competing land uses.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To achieve 30 by 30, we need a significant transformation of Singapore's agri-food sector.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As part of this transformation, SFA has recently embarked on the holistic master planning of the 390-hectare Lim Chu Kang area.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: It will take time for these plans to be implemented.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Shawn Huang asked if we could have poultry production in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Given our land, labour, energy and water constraints, we prefer to concentrate on farming food items that can be produced in a resource efficient and commercially sustainable manner.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: For example, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) reported that producing one kilogramme of chicken for meat would generate about three times that the CO2-equivalent emissions compared to some fish.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We currently have about 260 local farms producing food items that are commonly consumed and have local demand, such as eggs, fish and vegetables.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To Mr Edward Chia's question on our crisis stockpile, the Government works closely with industry partners to maintain stockpiles of essential food items in order to mitigate the impact of any unforeseen disruptions to our food supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: These stockpiles will help to stabilise supplies during periods of acute disruption as imports from other sources are ramped up.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As mentioned by Prime Minister Lee recently, the Government had begun to build up our stockpiles to a higher level at the early stage of the COVID-19 pandemic, as we were concerned with possible disruptions to our food supply, I have described our food security strategies to mitigate the risks of unavailability of supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: However, we will not be able to eliminate all risks.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: To do so would be costly and uneconomical.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will also not be able to isolate Singapore from the price fluctuations of food supply.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As we have seen in recent months, even countries with sizeable food production capabilities face higher food prices because of higher prices of feedstocks, fertilisers and transportation costs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Price control or subsidies for food, distorts business conditions and may not be financially sustainable.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: All Singaporean households would also have received $100 CDC voucher in May to help with daily expenses and the Deputy Prime Minister has already addressed many Parliamentary Questions on this issue, so I do not intend to repeat his points here.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Ms Jessica Tan asked about our support to businesses and consumers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The majority of poultry market stalls and chicken rice hawker stalls have remained open.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have also linked up affected hawkers and market stallholders with the Meat Traders Association to switch to frozen or thawed frozen chicken.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our businesses have shown resilience by adapting and pivoting to alternatives, as they have done so with previous disruptions over the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If needed, we will extend assistance and relieve the burden on businesses and households, as we have done so in the past.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Alex Yam asked about our engagement with the Malaysian government on the chicken export ban.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: SFA continues to keep in close contact with the Malaysian DVS.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: While our multi-pronged strategy has worked well in mitigating the impact of such disruptions, we remain vigilant and nimble in the execution of our strategy when new conditions emerge.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Businesses should similarly review their Business Continuity Plan and diversify their supplies.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Households and individuals too, can contribute to our food resilience by accommodating changes and pivoting to other food types when one is not available.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The critical success factor of our food security is the ability of Singaporeans – businesses, consumers, policy makers – together collectively, to adapt, adjust and remain resilient in the face of supply disruptions.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Together, we can and we will face any challenges that may come our way.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have one supplementary question for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In my course of engaging the public as well as stakeholders on our food resilience plan, suggestions like what Ms Pereira has offered, are often heard.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There were suggestions about using rooftops for community farming, using space in front of our void decks and allowing Singaporeans to plan and grow their own food for food resilience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Also, there were suggestions for other types of farming, such as permaculture for soil rehabilitation, crop rotation, so that we can improve our ecosystem and eco-diversity.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In many ways, they can contribute and add to our food resilience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But, as SFA, looks after food supply resilience, our priority must be to meet a significant proportion of our food supply needs, build up significant skillsets so that we have the production knowledge and capability onshore to support us in times of need.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, while we are developing our Lim Chu Kang masterplan, we will incorporate suggestions, such as, what Ms Pereira had offered.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, we also invite the public, the stakeholders, the businesses to join us in raising the productivity and production capabilities of our local agri-farm sector.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is, as Minister said, very concerning that there is still risk even with our multi-pronged approach.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, maybe I will turn my question around.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think Minister has done quite a bit of engagements with both businesses and and Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What is it that Singaporeans, individuals and businesses, what is it that we need to do more of to be able to support this strategy?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I think many of us have made many rounds at our wet markets, our coffee shops to survey and to understand the situation.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We – myself and my colleagues from NEA and SFA – have been reviewing and surveying constantly and regularly, so as to allow us to understand what is happening on the ground.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Which are the stores that remain open, what are they selling, how are they getting alternative sources?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: A nasi lemak stallholder said that: "I've learned to diversify, not just for chicken but for many of the major types of ingredients and to multiple suppliers, because during the COVID-19 period, we have seen how suppliers has not been able to cope".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, he has learnt to diversify to multiple suppliers.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We have also a "si yau gai", a soy sauce chicken, seller in my area, who has basically replaced his fresh chicken with frozen chicken.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We also have poultry stallholders who were selling chicken, fresh chicken and so on, converting to sell kampong chicken, black chicken and frozen chicken as well.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And I have a quintessential Hainanese chicken stallholder, who shared with me that she has switched to frozen but could not get the same taste as before and so their business has been affected.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And then, she showed me her very swollen fingers, saying, "This is what I have to go through to try to thaw many frozen chicken in order to try to get to the same recipe and same taste as before".

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I am sharing this as our stallholders have actually shown great resilience.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And even though they have not really recovered to pre-ban days, they are definitely trying.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And I think that is the kind of spirit that we would like to see and encourage Singaporean businesses, stallholders to have.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Sometimes, in the eagerness of helping them with financial assistance or other assistance, we must not undermine this resilience that we see.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And we also must not reverse some of the good business practices, the business continuity plans that they have started or implemented.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We should not unwind some of these things.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As a whole, I hope our businesses are able to diversify during peacetime, establish trade relations with more suppliers across different countries.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Diversify, so that we know if there is a bout of avian flu, we will not be affected in the same way, and I look at a having good business continuity plan.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Our businesses, small businesses, have shown resilience, adaptability and flexibility in different forms of meat and different ways of cooking – if you cannot do it in the boiled state, do it in the grilled way.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I think this will make us a lot more resilient.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As for individuals like ourselves here, we can always look for different types of cooking, different menus, different sources.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: And if you are able to again adapt to it, if you cannot buy it this week, just do not eat this form of meat.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If you cannot find chicken, let us go for other forms of proteins like eggs.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There are very good alternatives around and if you show some hardiness, then, as a whole, the whole country, the whole of Singapore, will have much better resilience against food disruptions.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, can import fees for live and chilled poultry from all approved suppliers be waived until Malaysia completely lifts its export restrictions on chicken?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The rest comes from countries like Thailand and Australia.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, is there any reason why we do not accredit other countries?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There are reasons because, as I mentioned, food safety is definitely one consideration.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: From time to time, countries are affected by zoonotic diseases, such as avian flu.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, our food security surveillance or food security review system has to take these factors into consideration and we do get into sometimes, protracted discussions with the relevant authorities, about how they are doing safety compartmentalisation, so that affected areas are not affecting the supply from the non-affected area.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I do not wish to go into further details here, but let me give you the assurance that we will support our businesses.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: In the pre-COVID-19 days, we used to go together with our trade associations to open up new areas and I think that the supplies from South America is one of the outcomes.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We go together, we decide on which are the areas that we want to focus our priorities on and we managed to establish the kind of trade links.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: As to why we are only getting from Malaysia, it is actually related to the first question.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Although we have accredited many other countries, but because of proximity, because of historical reasons of having associations with businesses between Singapore and Malaysia, we are very closely linked, with a long history of doing business together.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Malaysia continues to be an important source country for us.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I do not believe that we have any significant import fees that will hinder the establishment of a new market but if the Member has specific questions or issues with import fees or costs, please let us know, we will be happy to look into it.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: There will always be a cost competitive reason for importers to gravitate to the source market that is most competitive.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Sometimes, it is because it is the nearest, sometimes it is because it has an established logistics chain that can allow the goods to arrive in the shortest time.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Because of competition, they will be reluctant to try new areas that may increase the cost.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: The more conditions we impose on licenses, on business regulations, it will introduce rigidity, no doubt.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: But we may have to do it because it is a trade-off to encourage businesses or to require businesses to diversify.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, if we find that there is a strategic reason for us to do it, we will do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have two supplementary questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The first is a little bit shorter one.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Have the Malaysian authorities given any indication to SFA when they will review or, perhaps, end the current ban on chicken export?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The second is related to our food security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In our previous food security roadmap – I think this is 2013, 2014 – stockpiling was considered one of the core strategies for food security.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The last time the public was updated on our national stockpile was, I think, in March 2020, at the start of the pandemic and amidst panic buying.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing in his capacity then as Minister for Trade and Industry updated on the situation of our national stockpile.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Minister, therefore, update the House on our current stockpile situation, whether they remain robust and without jeopardising our negotiating position?

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Are we more resilient today, considering the two years of COVID-19 and the challenges brought about by the Ukraine conflict and global feedstock cost?

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: Second, about the update on food security roadmap, we work very closely with MTI, given the current situation and quite volatile conditions, many reasons, many factors to be concerned with.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: We will continue to work closely with MTI and we have done so, adjusting our stockpiling positions and stances.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: I would say that our businesses themselves have reacted very positively in also stockpiling for themselves.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: So, I think this is an area that we will continue to have the discussion within MSE, with MTI, on stockpiling and also with the downstream businesses on what they need or the amount of food that they need to stockpile.

speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
text: If there is a more specific question about the strategy on stockpiling, maybe the Member would like to address the question to MTI.
